reasoning: MDP-1 proved dispatch/execute/verify with a python worker written for the occasion. The target architecture puts the work into a harness behind the node's gateway. Until a directive travels crier -> node -> Hermes gateway -> result, the factory is still relaying through a script we wrote.

A directive is pushed to the node's crier inbox and reaches the Hermes gateway (session.create + prompt.submit), with the crier message id and the gateway session id both recorded. 2. The result returns over crier with a correlated dispatch id and the node's hostname. 3. A commit produced in the node is visible from the control host with the same sha. 4. foreman_note:
2026-11-04 probe on cf-node. (1) The node gateway was NOT running: /api/status reported gateway_running=false, gateway_state=null. Started with 'hermes gateway run' detached; it came up API-only ('WARNING gateway.run: No messaging platforms enabled'), now gateway_running=true, gateway_state=running. (2) The session API accepts no credential that exists on the node: /api/status answers 200 unauthenticated, but /api/health, /api/sessions and /api/agents return 401 for no auth, HTTP basic with the correctly parsed dashboard.basic_auth pair, Authorization: Bearer <dashboard password>, and X-API-Key <dashboard password>. /login and /auth/login return 405 to POST; /api/login returns 401. (3) Cause: config.yaml carries only dashboard.basic_auth (user node, 32-char password); there is no api_server block and no API_SERVER_KEY, so no API credential exists to present. scripts/node_gateway_auth.py writes basic_auth (making a public bind legal) but nothing mints a gateway API key. => AC1 needs a provisioning change: mint a per-node gateway API key, record it where the control host can read it, and present it. Not a live edit on cf-node.

Step 2, same probe session. (a) Minted API_SERVER_KEY into the node profile secret scope (48 chars, fingerprint fc795fcb); the running service did not pick it up, and after restarting the node's gateway with the env loaded, /api/health, /api/sessions and /api/agents still returned 401 — now with the useful body {error:unauthenticated, reason:no_cookie, login_url:/login}. So the node's API is COOKIE-authenticated, not bearer. (b) Login surface: GET /login renders a JS form (class=provider-form data-provider=basic, fields next/username/password). POST /login and /auth/login return 405; /auth/basic and /auth/provider/basic return 302 but set NO cookie (jar count 0), and the cookie-less API call still answers reason=no_cookie. The stored dashboard credential is a 32-char password; the control host's own config carries both password and password_hash fields, so a plaintext POST may simply not be the accepted form. (c) Conclusion for AC1: the node exposes a dashboard API, not a service API. Either the node must be given a real api_server credential the gateway accepts without a browser login, or the tick must be submitted through the harness CLI with tools and workspace present (CF-220). No live edit on cf-node will settle this; it is a provisioning contract question.

title: Node lifecycle: supervisor, renew, destroy/rebuild
reasoning: A node's gateway is started with nohup and dies on agent stop/renew; agent TTL is 4h unless renewed. A node that silently disappears is indistinguishable from a node that failed, and cancellation is only possible by killing the process group from a second exec (client kill and --timeout do NOT stop remote work).
acceptance_criteria: 1. The harness runs under a supervisor that restarts it and records restarts. 2. Agent TTL is renewed automatically while the node is active. 3. Cancelling a dispatch kills the process GROUP and the evidence shows it (job pid/pgid written by the job, killed, completion artifact absent after the deadline). 4. destroy then create reproduces the node from recorded commands with no manual step. 5. A node that dies mid-job causes redelivery, and idempotency prevents duplicated work.

title: P4 — GitReins guard refuses every documentation-only commit as DEGRADED PASS (lint scope is Python-only)
reasoning:
The GitReins guard cannot pass a documentation-only commit in this repo. `.gitreins/config.yaml`
sets `guards.allow_skips: false` and `lint_command: bash -n $(git ls-files "*.sh")`, but the lint
guard decides its scope from staged file extensions and reports `skip_reason=no staged files`
whenever no Python file is staged, which makes Tier 1 `DEGRADED PASS`; the repo policy then refuses
the commit and no commit object is created.

Measured 2026-10-30 on a docs-only change (README.md + docs/audits/*.md + board events.jsonl) from
worktree `~/worktrees/code-factory-readme-20261030-182833`, tip cc0a1e4:

- `git commit -F msg` -> guard log `.gitreins/logs/guard-20261030T212945.104300Z.log`
- `overall: PASS (DEGRADED — skipped checks)`, `guards: 3 (0 failed, 1 skipped)`,
  `skipped_steps: - lint: no staged files`, detail line `No Python files staged`
- `secrets` PASS (gitleaks clean), `tests (full)` PASS (exit 0, `SELFTEST: PASS`, which runs
  `bash -n` over every script internally)
- `git log --oneline -1` after the attempt still shows the pre-commit tip: no commit was created

The consequence is that every docs and readme lane change, and every board-only commit, needs a
hook bypass to land. That is exactly the kind of skip the repo's own gate is meant to refuse, so
the gate must be able to grade a non-Python diff instead of skipping it.

Acceptance criteria:

1. A documentation-only commit (no .py and no .sh changed) completes through the guard with Tier 1
   `PASS`, not `DEGRADED PASS`, from a clean worktree of this repo; a re-runnable reproduction is
   `git commit --allow-empty -m probe` on a scratch branch with a README line added.
2. The guard log for that run shows the lint gate executed rather than skipped, and names what it
   executed (`bash -n` targets or an explicit "no lint targets in this diff" that the repo policy
   accepts).
3. No bypass (`--no-verify`, `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`) is used in the reproduction, and the
   resulting commit exists on the branch.
4. `bash tests/selftest.sh` still passes and the guard's secrets and full-test legs still run.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A documentation-only commit completes through the guard with Tier 1 PASS, not DEGRADED PASS, from a clean worktree.
2. The guard log shows the lint gate executed and names its targets instead of skipping.
3. No bypass (--no-verify, core.hooksPath=/dev/null) is used and the commit exists on the branch.
4. bash tests/selftest.sh still passes and the secrets and full-test legs still run.
foreman_note:
Root cause measured 2026-10-30 in gitreins 0.17.1: engine/guard_manager.py::_check_lint builds py_files from changed_files filtered to '*.py' and never reads guards.lint_command; with no staged .py it returns GuardResult(skipped=True, skip_reason='no staged files'). Experiment in this repo's worktree: staging any *.py makes the identical tree return Tier 1 PASS with 'lint — ok'; staging none (every docs/README/board/shell-only commit) returns DEGRADED PASS and, with allow_skips:false, the commit is refused. So the blast radius is every non-Python commit in this repo, not documentation only. grade_full_tree exists but is CLI-only (gitreins guard --full), there is no config key; repo-side options are (a) allow_skips:true — weakens the gate, (b) invoke the hook as 'gitreins guard --full' so lint grades the tree's four .py files and names them — no weakening, local hook change, not shippable in-repo, (c) upstream: make the lint lane honour lint_command or accept a non-.py scope. Evidence: docs/audits/code-factory-readme-2026-10-30-20-29-25.md and guard logs guard-20261030T231404 and guard-20261030T232504.

Sync lane 2026-11-03: reproduced. A docs+board-only commit (docs/BOARD.md, new docs/audits/ artifact, two board rows) was refused twice by the pre-commit guard at 15:15:17Z and 15:15:57Z. Both runs: secrets clean, tests (full) PASS; the block is DEGRADED PASS from lint skipping with reason 'no staged files' / 'No Python files staged'. guards.allow_skips is false in .gitreins/config.yaml. The work was committed with the documented core.hooksPath bypass and the bypass is disclosed in that commit message. Row stays pending: the guard still refuses docs-only changes.

title: Lane workdir is a target, not a local path: user@host, ssh/sftp/ftp and bunker forms
reasoning: Five enabled satellites had workdirs resolving to $HOME, so they read the wrong board. The repository only knew how to mkdir a local path; remote execution needs the workdir to address another host.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `python3 scripts/lane_target.py parse <target>` accepts every documented form: absolute or ~ path, local:/path, user@host:/path, ssh://user@host[:port]/path, sftp/ftp/ftps/rsync URLs, bunker://<agent>/path; an unparseable or relative local path exits 2 with a message naming the accepted forms.
2. `verify` on a LOCAL target fails when the git top level is $HOME (the stand-in locator defect), when the target is not a checkout, has no remote, or is on a detached HEAD; it passes on a real checkout with a remote and an attached branch.
3. `verify` on a REMOTE target is reported as `remote-structural-only` and exits 3 unless `--allow-remote` is passed, so a remote workdir is never silently reported as verified.
4. `scripts/configure_family.py` only creates directories for LOCAL targets and registers a remote target verbatim.
5. `python3 -B tests/test_lane_target.py` prints OK and `bash tests/selftest.sh` prints SELFTEST: PASS (section 11 covers this contract).

Two of the enabled satellite lanes (code-factory-docs, -pm, -qa, -readme, -sync) had workdirs that resolved to /home/kara, so they read the home repo board instead of this project. Constraining workdir to a local directory string was the cause; the target model plus the home-repo rejection is the fix. Bane directive 2026-11-03: "fix the workdir bug by including the ability that the path is not just the file path but more like ftp path that include user and server etc".
worker_summary: lane_target.py parses/verifies local and remote workdir targets; configure_family.py mkdirs only local targets. tests/test_lane_target.py 22 tests OK; selftest section 11 PASS.
foreman_note: Implemented with the CF-007 floor work in one commit. Home-repo rejection is the regression guard for the five satellites that read /home/kara.

title: P4 — node-create.sh stage-2 cannot fail: four swallowed bunker calls followed by an unconditional ok staged, plus a fixed /tmp/spawn.log shared by every lane
reasoning: Measured 2026-11-03 on a live node (bunker-las-03) by this lane and re-read at tip 820e8134. scripts/node-create.sh:38-46 runs one mkdir exec, three `bunker cp` copies and one chmod exec, each with `>/dev/null 2>&1`, then line 48 prints ok "staged" "project-node.sh + harness/install-$HARNESS.sh" unconditionally. Nothing in the block can produce FAIL: if a copy fails (missing harness file, closed agent, full disk inside the node) the script still claims staging succeeded and the error reappears later as 'FAIL provision — node reported FAIL', which misattributes a control-host transfer failure to the node's provisioning. Second defect in the same block: the spawn log is the fixed path /tmp/spawn.log (line 35), so two lanes provisioning concurrently overwrite each other's only diagnostic, and a stale log from another lane can be printed as this run's failure. Both are AGENTS.md rule-2/rule-5 adjacent (a step that cannot fail, and a step that is not collision-safe).
acceptance_criteria: 1. A failing copy (e.g. harness adapter removed between the -x test and the cp, or a node whose target directory is read-only) produces `FAIL staged` naming the artifact that failed to land, and no `PASS provision` follows. 2. The spawn log path is unique per run (contains the agent id or a mktemp path) and is named in the failure output. 3. tests/selftest.sh carries a fixture proving the staged-failure path can go red while the happy path stays green. 4. bash tests/selftest.sh prints SELFTEST: PASS at the fixed tip.

reasoning:
Measured 2026-11-03 by the code-factory releng-QA lane (tick code-factory-releng-qa-2026-11-03-15-39-07) at origin/main ac30ceb, no node and no network.

(1) `scripts/disk_floor.py` accepts decimal sizes by design (docstring :17) but converts them with `int(float(...))` (:66) and `int(raw)` (:55), so a floor is truncated DOWN, never up and never refused: `resolve --cli 5.9G --explain` prints `{"role": "worker", "floor_gib": 5, "source": "cli"}` and a config `default = "5.9G"` prints the same 5 with `source: config-default`. `5.1G`, `5.5G` and `5.9G` are therefore the same policy, and 5.0-5.9 are one number.

(2) The module's own contract states the opposite intent: 'Anything else fails closed (exit 2) rather than silently falling back to a default — a typo must not lower a floor.' A truncated decimal is exactly a silent lowering, and the `source` field it prints ('cli', 'config-default') asserts the operator's value was used, which hides the substitution.

(3) The consequence reaches admission, not just the printed JSON: `require_disk` (scripts/lib.sh:35-44) compares `df`'s float free-space with the integer the resolver returned. With a `df` shim reporting 5.5 GB free and a floor requested as 5.9G, the row reads `PASS  disk — 5.5 GB free (floor 5 GB)` and the admission returns 0 — a host below the operator's floor is admitted, and the printed floor is the truncated number, so the mismatch is invisible in the very output that is supposed to make the refusal falsifiable (CF-007's premise).

(4) The same value feeds the `--apply` path (`project-node.sh:144` require_disk, `:107-113` floor resolution), so this is an acceptance decision, not a label.

(5) Not established here: which of the two repairs the project wants (preserve the decimal through a float comparison, or refuse decimals outright with exit 2). The row requires one of them plus a test, and names the docstring that has to agree.

2. Distinct decimals produce distinct enforcement: `5.1G`, `5.5G`, `5.9G` yield three different floors (or three refusals), proven by one `require_disk` arm per value against a `df` shim reporting 5.5 GB free — 5.1 PASSes, 5.9 must not.

3. A numbered `tests/selftest.sh` section asserts those arms and FAILS on the pre-fix `scripts/disk_floor.py` (paste both runs and both exit codes into the evidence artifact).

4. The docstring, `--help`, and any spec/README text quoting the accepted forms state the rounding policy the code actually implements — the sentence 'a typo must not lower a floor' is true of the shipped resolver.

5. `bash tests/selftest.sh` prints `SELFTEST: PASS`, `scripts/boardctl validate` prints `RESULT: OK`, the board parses every line with unique ids, and the closing commit is pushed with `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` = 0.

title: P3 — clone_lane.py mints a lane with the source lane's cooldown and pin, and disables a live lane on re-run
reasoning:
Measured by the code-factory-qa tick code-factory-qa-2026-11-04-00-07-40 at origin/main d586336, in a detached worktree (git worktree add --detach <scratch> origin/main), probe executed from the repo root.

scripts/clone_lane.py is the shipped tool that mints a lane row by cloning a canonical sibling (docstring: the scheduler's lane-onboarding gate refuses every workdir for docs/readme/perf/review families, so cloning a live row is the only way to give a new project the same shape). It reads the source row with SELECT * and copies the WHOLE row (`row = dict(src)`), overriding only name, workdir, namespace_id, parent, enabled=0, repo_url, prompt_mode, the three last_tick_* fields, consecutive_failures, created_at and updated_at. Everything else is inherited verbatim: cooldown_s, cooldown_pin_s, cooldown_pin_by, cooldown_pin_at, the bump_* set, board_rows_seen/board_open_seen and the qa/pm/sync/dogfood zero-output counters.

That inheritance is not theoretical: 868 of the 876 rows in ~/.hermes/coding-hermes/scheduler.db carry cooldown_pin_s > 0 today (values include 604800 = 7d, 21600 = 6h), so a clone of almost any live lane starts its life pinned. The cloned lane is written enabled=0, so the pin is invisible until an operator enables it — and enabling does not clear cooldown_pin_s, so the new lane's first tick is up to seven days away with no output and no error. That is the same user-visible outcome CF-134 (P1) describes, reached through a different mechanism.

Two more defects in the same write path, both reproduced by the probe: (1) when the destination name already exists the tool prints "already exists — configuring it instead of creating" and then UPDATEs every cloned column, including enabled=0, so re-running it to re-point a live lane silently DISABLES that lane and overwrites its own 900 s cooldown with the source's 604800 s; (2) repo_url is hardcoded to local:~/code-factory and ignores --workdir entirely, so a clone whose workdir is anywhere else is written with a repo_url that contradicts its own workdir — exactly the intra-family disagreement scripts/lane_target.py's CF-091 check exists to reject.

Boundary against existing rows: CF-134 is the pin VALUES freezing the fleet and is fixed by unpinning rows; this is the mint tool's write path, which re-imports pins from any source row, so CF-134 can close and a single clone_*_lane invocation reintroduces one. CF-085 (complete) fixed repo_url INHERITANCE for satellites at mint time; this is a hardcoded path that ignores both the source and --workdir. No row on the board mentions clone_lane.py (census over id/title/reasoning at d586336: 0 hits).
acceptance_criteria:
1. Repro on the current tree: the row's probe prints new-lane with cooldown_s=604800 and cooldown_pin_s=604800 inherited from the 604800 s source lane, and prints live-lane (created enabled=1, cooldown_s=900) as enabled=0, cooldown_s=604800, cooldown_pin_s=604800 after the tool is re-run on the existing name.
2. After the fix, `scripts/clone_lane.py --from <src> --to <new>` writes cooldown_s=900 (or the explicit --cooldown-s value) and leaves cooldown_pin_s NULL, cooldown_pin_by='' and cooldown_pin_at='' on the new lane regardless of the source row's values; the probe's new-lane line must read cooldown_s=900 and an empty pin.
3. After the fix, re-running the tool on an EXISTING lane preserves that lane's enabled flag and its own cooldown_s; an overwrite requires --force, and the tool prints the field names it changed. The probe's live-lane line must read enabled=1, cooldown_s=900.
4. After the fix, repo_url is derived from --workdir (`git -C <workdir> rev-parse --show-toplevel`) or accepted explicitly via --repo-url, so a clone whose workdir is not a ~/code-factory checkout never prints local:/home/kara/code-factory; the probe's two written rows show repo_url matching $d/wd.

AGENTS.md and docs/BOARD.md both describe the board as append-only, one JSON object per line, and the fleet's skill doctrine forbids rewriting a tracked JSONL board through a JSON slurp/dump. What changed is the raw bytes of historical lines — the legacy rows written as `{"id": 1, "timestamp": ...}` (space after the colon) now read compact. title: P3 — the layer-00 reach probe reports 000 (unreachable) for a URL that answered 200: the CF-037 fix shape discards curl's printed code when --max-time cuts the transfer
reasoning: Measured 2026-11-04 at published tip eada934 with a portable fixture (no external network): a local `python3 -m http.server` serving a 100 KB body, probed with `curl --limit-rate 20k --max-time 1`. Result: `curl_printed_code=200 curl_rc=28 script_value=000`. scripts/project-node.sh:190-195 (the shape CF-037 introduced) is `if ! c=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 8 "$u" 2>/dev/null); then c=000; fi`: curl writes the status it already received (200) and then exits 28 when --max-time cuts the body, and the `if !` throws that printed value away and records 000. The FAIL row then reads `reach:<url> — -> 000`, which is indistinguishable from DNS failure or no egress. Observed in the wild on 2026-11-03's node: layer 00 printed `FAIL reach:https://pypi.org/simple/ — -> 000` in the same run whose layer 40 printed `PASS repo_clone … @ df40870`, and three direct probes on that node returned http=200 at 9.4-10.0 s, aborted mid-body. A stranger's next move is to chase DNS or egress on a node that just cloned over the same network, and the FAIL names no value to supply. Distinct from CF-037 (the `|| echo 000` deformation, fixed) and CF-072 (that deformation in three other scripts): this is the replacement idiom's false-negative mode, and it fires on a REACHABLE URL.

title: P4 — the section-mapping gate counts DISTINCT numbers at column 0 only: a duplicate-numbered section and an indented section header both land uncounted while the gate prints RESULT: OK

CF-198 (complete) shipped `docs/audits/cf198-section-mapping.sh` and its selftest §39 arm, whose stated purpose is that "the next section that lands cannot leave the table or the count behind" (CF-198 AC1). The census behind it is `grep -oE '^say "[0-9]+\.' tests/selftest.sh | grep -oE '[0-9]+' | sort -nu`: it counts DISTINCT numbers, and it only sees headers that start at column 0.

Two spellings therefore land uncounted, both measured on throwaway copies of the current tree:
- a second section carrying an ALREADY-USED number (`say "45. ..."` appended): the tree then holds 50 at-column headers, `sort -nu` collapses the pair, and the gate prints `arms_plan=49 arms_tree=49` / `RESULT: OK` (rc 0). Duplicate numbering is exactly the copy-paste error the mapping table exists to catch: two arms share one plan row.
- an INDENTED header (`if true; then\n  say "47. ..."\nfi` appended, a plausible shape for a conditional arm): the `^say` regex does not match it, so the gate again prints `arms_plan=49 arms_tree=49` / `RESULT: OK` (rc 0) while the tree carries one more arm than it counts.

The in-repo gates do not catch either arm: on a copy whose plan numbered-section claim was mutated from 46 to 47 the suite still prints `SELFTEST: PASS` (284 PASS rows), and the mapping gate itself is the instrument that stays green. So both red arms are silent: no named FAIL row, exit 0.

Scope boundary, deduplicated by class against the landed board (0 hits for "duplicate section|indented section|sort -nu"): CF-113 (pending) owns the lettered-arm blindness of `cf099-prd-drift-probe.sh --sections-only`; CF-186 (pending) owns the §7c census arm that the CF-151 landing deleted; CF-198 (complete) shipped the instrument graded here. This row owns the two spellings the instrument's own regex and de-duplication cannot see; it is not a re-filing of any of those.

Sequence of measurement: `bash docs/audits/cf198-section-mapping.sh` on the pristine tree prints `arms_plan=49 arms_tree=49` / `RESULT: OK` (control); appending a duplicate-numbered header gives `at_column_headers=50` with `RESULT: OK`; appending an indented header gives `indented_headers=1` with `RESULT: OK`. title: A real foreman directive makes the node harness run 39 minutes and return 36 bytes, and nothing records what it was doing
acceptance_criteria:
1. A directive that takes longer than the poll interval produces a progress record an operator can read WHILE it runs: at minimum the last tool call and its elapsed time, written at a fixed cadence.
2. When such a run is killed, the record says what it was doing at the moment of the kill, so the failure is attributable rather than 'it hung'.
3. The node session store shows the conversation so far on a killed run: today a 39-minute run leaves exactly one message (the user prompt) and no assistant or tool rows.
4. A test reproduces the hang with a directive of comparable size and asserts that progress was recorded before the deadline, so this cannot regress silently.
foreman_note:
Evidence, 2026-11-04. The durable path started job-1793881486-969735cc on cf-node with the real 4,046-byte foreman directive at 07:24:56 and killed it at 08:03:58: rc=124 after 2342s (39 minutes). Its out.log is 36 bytes and contains only 'session_id: 20261105_042456_716a72'. The node's state.db has exactly ONE message for that session — the user prompt — so no assistant or tool activity was persisted for the whole run. The same node answers 'ALIVE-CHECK' in seconds for a short prompt (session 20261105_050420_fe00cc), and the 400s boundary job returned BOUNDARY-CROSSED, so the harness and the job model both work; it is this class of directive that hangs. Nothing in the run can be attributed beyond 'it hung', which is why the row asks for progress records rather than more retries.

Implemented and observed 2026-11-04. run.sh starts a heartbeat that appends '<UTC time> hp=<pid> <elapsed> <cmdline>' to progress.log every 20s; the dispatcher polls that line and logs it when it changes. Live example from job job-1793884459-472317b8: '13:14:48 hp=1292325 00:20 timeout 150 /home/bunker-cf-node/.local/bin/hermes chat -q Write a 600 word essay about tundra. -Q' then '00:40' on the next line, finishing rc=0 at 55s. Three defects were found and fixed while making it true: GNU timeout runs the command in its own process group (so a run.sh pgid scan reports idle for a live harness), ps --no-headers is unsupported in the node image, and ps output contains non-UTF8 bytes that crashed subprocess text=True at three call sites (now errors=replace). AC1 is met and observed; AC2 (what it was doing at the kill) follows from the same record but has not yet been captured on a killed real run; AC3 (session store shows only the user message on a killed run) is still true and unfixed.

Kill capture, 2026-11-04. Re-ran the real 4,046-byte directive through the durable path with the heartbeat live. Job job-1793885085-89c9fe3d: started 08:24:56, killed rc=124 at 08:49:01 after 1447s. The record names the position at the kill: '13:48:36 hp=1292809 23:41 timeout 1440 .../hermes chat -q [Scheduler tick: diag-node-1] ...' — 23m41s inside the same process, and at NO point during 24 minutes did a child process appear (no git, no python3, no bash), so no tool ran. AC2 is now met: the record says what the run was doing when it was killed. Attribution of WHY is narrowed: the node-to-proxy leg is not at fault — measured from the control host against the same proxy, 4.4KB (5.9s), 20KB (2.7s), 60KB (3.4s) and a streaming request (180 chunks, 3.4s) all return 200; the tick prefix alone returns PREFIX-OK on the node in seconds. What remains is the harness's own agent loop, which is invisible because it runs tools in-process and persists nothing until exit. Next step is harness-level logging, not more transport work.

title: The node harness raises its stream read timeout to 1800s, so a stalled model stalls the job for half an hour
acceptance_criteria:
1. A stalled upstream produces an error and a non-zero exit within a bounded time, instead of a run that sits until an external kill.
2. The bound is configurable and its effective value is logged at request start, so an operator can tell 'waiting' from 'hung'.
3. A test simulates an upstream that accepts the connection and sends no bytes, and asserts the harness fails within the bound.
4. The failure is recorded in the session store, not only on stdout, so a killed run still shows why.
foreman_note:
Found by harness-level logging on cf-node (2026-11-04). Ran the real 4,079-byte directive under 'hermes chat -v' with a 150s cap; the verbose log shows the exact stall: '06:05:32 API Request - Model: hermes, Messages: 1, Tools: 18', 'Total message size: ~5,386 tokens', then 'agent.chat_completion_helpers - DEBUG - Local provider detected (http://100.97.236.14:8775/v1) — stream read timeout raised to 1800s', and NOTHING until '06:07:52 - Received signal 15' (140 seconds of silence, ended by the test cap). So the harness itself sets a 1800s stream read timeout for local providers — which is why the two real runs sat 1447s and 2342s. The upstream stall is the trigger; the 1800s default is why it looks like a hung job instead of a failed request. Same proxy answers 4.4KB/20KB/60KB and a streaming request in 3-6s from the control host, so the difference in the harness request is its 18-tool schema payload and the streaming tool-call path.

Ruled out (2026-11-04), each measured rather than assumed. (1) Payload size: 4.4KB 5.9s, 20KB 2.7s, 60KB 3.4s — all 200. (2) Streaming: 200, 180 chunks, 3.4s. (3) Tool schemas: stream+tools at 2 and 18 schemas returned first byte in 5.9s and 4.7s. (4) Large responses through the NODE's own harness: a 1200-word essay (10,800 bytes) rc=0 in under 150s. So neither size, streaming, tool schemas, nor long output triggers it. What the failing run shows is different: the verbose log stops at 'API Request - Model: hermes, Messages: 1, Tools: 18 ... ~5,386 tokens' and then produces NO first byte for 140s, so the stall is before the first response token for that request shape, not during a tool loop (no tool calls are ever logged and no child process ever appears). The remaining unknown is the exact request body the harness emits; capturing it is the next step, and the proxy's BrokenPipe at the same timestamp is the other end of the same event.

Exact request captured (2026-11-04). Added capture_request() to the proxy; it now appends the body a node actually sends to ~/.hermes/logs/cf-inference-requests.jsonl. Ran the real directive through the node harness with a 120s cap: rc=124, 36 bytes again, and the capture recorded exactly one request — 69,163 bytes, 2 messages, 18 tools, stream=true, keys [max_tokens, messages, model, stream, stream_options, tools]. That is 69KB against my largest successful probe of 60KB, and it is the first request shape carrying stream_options, which none of my reconstructions had. Replay of the captured body was blocked: the control-host replay returned 401, so the token I extracted from cf-node-tokens.json does not match the one the node is configured with — that mismatch is itself recorded here rather than worked around. Next step is a verbatim replay FROM the node using its own configured credential, with the capture cap raised from 20KB to the full body so nothing is truncated.

Verbatim replay attempt, 2026-11-04 — and the upstream is now the suspect. Capture raised to the full body: the node's real request is 69,163 bytes (68,907 chars) with 2 messages, 18 tools, stream=true, stream_options present, and the capture is written on every attempt, which proves the proxy DOES read the whole 69KB from the node — the request arrives, so the stall is downstream of the proxy's body read. Replayed that exact body FROM THE NODE using the node's own credential (CF_PROXY_API_KEY in ~/.hermes/.env, never printed): urllib fails in 0.4s with [Errno 32] Broken pipe. Attempted the same replay from the control host and got 401 for every value in ~/.hermes/secrets/cf-node-tokens.json, while the node's own credential authenticates fine — so that file is not the authority the proxy honours and my host-side probes were never speaking as the node. Establishes two facts and one next step: (a) the node's request reaches and is fully read by the proxy; (b) the proxy forwards to the control host's gateway at 127.0.0.1:8642, which is the remaining upstream and the only component not yet measured with this body. Next: measure :8642 directly with the same 69KB body using the gateway credential read at runtime from the hermes secret env, under the current host load, and record first-byte time; if it stalls there, the fault is the gateway under load, not the node, not the proxy, not the transport.

ROOT CAUSE LOCATED 2026-11-04, from the proxy's own usage log. The proxy's _forward() does urllib r.read() — it BUFFERS the whole upstream response before sending a single byte to the node, even when the client asked for stream=true. Measured consequence: one chat request logged '07:18:18 status=0 IncompleteRead secs=1289.38 model=hermes', and the maximum recorded chat duration is 2140.26s (35 minutes). So the sequence is: node sends 69KB (arrives, proven by capture) -> proxy forwards to the control host's gateway at 127.0.0.1:8642 -> the gateway takes 20-35 minutes to produce this turn -> the proxy holds the socket and delivers nothing -> the node's harness waits with its 1800s stream timeout -> the job wall (1447s, 2342s) kills it first. Nothing is wrong with the node, the tailnet, the payload size, the tool schemas, or the proxy's admission: the node's inference is being served by a saturated control-host gateway, and every layer above it hides that fact. Two fixes now have names: (1) the proxy must pass SSE through as it arrives instead of buffering, so the harness sees progress and the 1800s wait becomes a real first-byte; (2) node inference must not queue behind the control host's own load — it needs its own lane or provider, since the whole point of CF-002 is that nodes think without keys, not that they think at the control host's pace.

FIX 1 IMPLEMENTED AND VERIFIED 2026-11-04: the proxy now passes SSE through as it arrives instead of buffering the whole turn (_forward streams when the request body says stream=true, sends headers immediately, writes and flushes each 4096-byte chunk, and logs first_byte + streamed on the usage row). Verification: a node chat through the pass-through logged 'status=200 streamed=True first=0.0 secs=5.4 bytes=1354' and the node returned STREAM-OK, so the node now sees tokens as they are produced rather than after the whole generation. What this does NOT fix: the upstream gateway still takes 20-35 minutes to produce the foreman turn (measured 1289.38s and max 2140.26s before the change), so a real directive still exceeds its wall. It converts 'the node sees nothing for 1800s' into 'the node sees a live stream that is too slow' — which is the difference between an unattributable hang and a capacity problem with a number on it. title: P2 - the fleet dispatcher runs whatever code was on disk when it started, with no liveness check: a stale process reported a NEGATIVE job duration and its diagnosis blamed the carrier for slicing a prompt it never sliced
reasoning: Measured 2026-11-05 while proving the dispatch carrier end to end on cf-node. fleet-dispatcher.service (systemd --user) started 07:06:41 -0500; its file /home/kara/crier-fleet/dispatcher.py was last modified 08:14:19 -0500, i.e. 68 minutes LATER. The running process therefore executed pre-08:14 code while every reading of the file described the newer one. Two false conclusions came out of that gap, both in this session: (1) the dispatch log printed 'job <id> finished rc=0 after -13s' and 'after -14s' -- a negative elapsed that the file on disk cannot produce, because the current dispatch_durable() takes t_start = time.time() BEFORE its poll loop and logs time.time() - t_start; (2) an earlier tick's reply asserted the prompt 'was sliced at ~507 bytes', which a controlled experiment disproves for current code: a 1994-byte --text-file directive arrived byte-identical on the node (task.txt 1994 bytes, BEGIN-MARKER-7f3a and END-MARKER-9c1d both present), and a 184-byte directive arrived at exactly 184 bytes. After restarting the unit (new pid 4007455, started 13:48:59, now later than the file mtime) the same dispatch logged 'finished rc=0 after 16s' -- positive, as written. The defect is not the duration arithmetic; it is that nothing on the box can tell you which code a long-lived poller is running, so a stale process silently redefines the product under every subsequent measurement.
acceptance_criteria: 1. The dispatcher records the identity of the code it is running at startup (file mtime + sha256 of dispatcher.py) and stamps it on every job line it writes, so a log reader can tell which revision produced a measurement without guessing. 2. One command answers 'is the running dispatcher stale?' -- compare the process's own start time (from /proc or systemd) against dispatcher.py's mtime and exit non-zero when the file is newer -- and it is wired into the unit's readiness or a health probe, not left as a script nobody runs. 3. Proven in BOTH directions: with the current process the check exits 0; after `touch dispatcher.py` (or a process started before a file edit) it exits non-zero and names both timestamps. 4. A restart is safe and proven so: no in-flight job is abandoned unacked, and a job dispatched immediately after the restart completes with a positive duration.

Related but distinct: CF-206 (code-factory classified as docs) and CF-241 (the CF-206 patch has no applicable target because fleet_ops_check.py is tracked in no commit). 4) Second negative control, the one the fix could break: a fixture tree containing .coding-hermes/board/schema.sql AND a data.db must still report check=backup — the harness-dir exclusion must not swallow a real store that happens to sit beside it.
